title: Jira vs Plane
comparison_markdown:
# Jira vs Plane (2026)

## Overview
Jira and Plane are two project management tools that help teams track and manage their work. This comparison is useful for teams currently using Jira who are looking for a more cost-effective or customizable solution, and are considering switching to Plane for its self-hosted and free features. The core use case for both tools is issue tracking and project management, and the key reason someone would switch is to reduce costs or gain more control over their data.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Jira is a paid tool with a per-user monthly fee, while Plane is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: With Plane, teams have full ownership and control over their data, while Jira stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: Plane requires more technical expertise to set up and configure, while Jira offers a more user-friendly onboarding process.
* Scalability: Jira is designed to handle large and complex projects, while Plane is better suited for smaller to medium-sized teams.
* Integration difference: Jira has a more extensive library of integrations with third-party tools, while Plane has a more limited but growing list of integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Jira | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.75-$14.50/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $387.50-$725/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,550-$2,900/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Jira:**
* Pros:
	+ User-friendly interface
	+ Extensive library of integrations
	+ Scalable for large projects
	+ Robust reporting and analytics
	+ Good customer support
* Cons:
	+ Expensive, especially for large teams
	+ Limited customization options
	+ Data stored on proprietary servers
	+ Can be overwhelming for small teams
**Plane:**
* Pros:
	+ Free and self-hosted
	+ Full data ownership and control
	+ Customizable and flexible
	+ Suitable for small to medium-sized teams
	+ Open-source community
* Cons:
	+ Requires technical expertise to set up
	+ Limited integrations with third-party tools
	+ May not be suitable for large or complex projects
	+ Limited customer support
	+ Still in development, with some features missing

## When to Choose Each
Jira is a good choice for large teams or complex projects that require a high degree of scalability and integration with third-party tools. It is also suitable for teams who are already familiar with the tool and have invested in its ecosystem. On the other hand, Plane is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams who want a free and self-hosted solution with full data ownership and control. It is also suitable for teams who are looking for a customizable and flexible tool that can be tailored to their specific needs.

## Migration Path
1. Export your data from Jira in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up a Plane instance on your own server or use a hosted solution.
3. Use the Plane import tool to import your data from the Jira export file.
4. Configure Plane to match your team's workflow and needs.
5. Test and validate the migration to ensure that all data has been transferred correctly.

## Our Take
Plane is not yet production-ready for most users, as it is still in development and lacks some key features. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Plane does not yet have a built-in reporting and analytics tool, which may be a deal-breaker for some teams. However, for small to medium-sized teams who are looking for a free and self-hosted solution with full data ownership and control, Plane is definitely worth considering, and we recommend switching from Jira to Plane if you do not need the advanced features and scalability of Jira.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who do not need advanced features like reporting and analytics.
* Teams who require full data ownership and control.
* Teams who are looking for a free and self-hosted solution.
* Teams who do not need integration with third-party tools.
* Teams who are comfortable with setting up and configuring their own server.

## FAQ
### Is Plane free?
Yes, Plane is free and self-hosted, with no per-user fees.
### Can I migrate my data from Jira to Plane?
Yes, you can export your data from Jira in CSV or JSON format and import it into Plane using the Plane import tool.
### Is Plane suitable for large teams?
No, Plane is not yet suitable for large teams or complex projects, as it lacks some key features and scalability.
### Can I customize Plane to match my team's workflow?
Yes, Plane is highly customizable and flexible, and can be tailored to match your team's specific needs.
### Does Plane have a mobile app?
Not yet, but the Plane team is working on developing a mobile app for future release.

title: Trello vs WeKan
comparison_markdown:
# Trello vs WeKan

## Overview

Trello is a visual kanban board tool from Atlassian, simple and beginner-friendly. WeKan is an open-source kanban board offering the same card/list/board model without vendor dependency.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Trello paid plans start at $5/user/month; WeKan is completely free
- **Data control**: WeKan runs on your own server; Trello data lives on Atlassian infrastructure
- **Features**: Trello has a larger Power-Ups marketplace; WeKan covers core kanban features
- **Setup**: Trello requires zero setup; WeKan requires a server
- **Customization**: WeKan open-source code can be extended; Trello cannot

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Trello | WeKan |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $5+/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Trello

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### WeKan

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [wekan/wekan](https://github.com/wekan/wekan) * ~20k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Trello if:** Trello suits individuals and small teams wanting instant zero-setup kanban with integrations to Slack, Google Drive, and GitHub.

**Choose WeKan if:** WeKan is ideal for teams wanting full data ownership or air-gapped deployments.

## Migration Path

Export Trello boards as JSON, then use WeKan Trello importer in Settings to recreate boards, lists, and cards.

## Our Take

WeKan is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Trello tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your WeKan instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Trello, switching to self-hosted WeKan will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Trello until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Trello paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is WeKan free to use?
Yes. WeKan is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Trello to WeKan?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Trello data, follow the WeKan import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does WeKan get regular updates?
Yes. WeKan has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use WeKan without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if WeKan development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Trello](https://trello.com) and [WeKan](https://wekan.github.io) before making decisions.*
meta_description: WeKan is a free, self-hosted alternative to Trello. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

title: Dropbox vs Nextcloud
comparison_markdown:
# Dropbox vs Nextcloud (2026)

## Overview
Dropbox and Nextcloud are two popular cloud storage solutions that enable users to store, share, and collaborate on files. This comparison is ideal for individuals and teams seeking a reliable and secure platform for their file management needs, with a key reason to switch being the desire for greater control over data ownership and costs. The core use case for both tools is file storage and sharing, with the primary difference lying in their approach to data ownership and hosting.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Dropbox offers a range of pricing plans, while Nextcloud is free and open-source, with costs limited to server maintenance and upkeep.
* Data ownership: Nextcloud allows users to retain full ownership of their data, whereas Dropbox's terms of service grant the company certain rights to user content.
* Setup complexity: Dropbox is generally easier to set up and use, with a more streamlined user interface, while Nextcloud requires more technical expertise to configure and manage.
* Scalability: Nextcloud is highly scalable, with support for large numbers of users and files, while Dropbox's scalability is limited by its pricing plans and storage capacity.
* Integration: Nextcloud offers integration with a wider range of third-party apps and services, including calendar and contact management tools, while Dropbox's integrations are more limited.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Dropbox | Nextcloud |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $9.99-$16.58/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $499.50-$829.00/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,998.00-$3,316.00/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Dropbox:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Wide range of integrations with third-party apps
* Robust security and backup features
* Limited control over data ownership
* Cost can be prohibitively expensive for large teams
**Nextcloud:**
* High degree of control over data ownership and security
* Highly scalable and customizable
* Wide range of integrations with third-party apps
* Can be complex to set up and manage
* Limited support for certain file types and formats

## When to Choose Each
When to choose Dropbox: Dropbox is ideal for small to medium-sized teams that require a simple, easy-to-use file storage and sharing solution. It is particularly well-suited for teams that do not require a high degree of control over their data and are willing to pay a premium for convenience and ease of use. Dropbox is also a good choice for teams that require a wide range of integrations with third-party apps and services.
When to choose Nextcloud: Nextcloud is ideal for large teams or organizations that require a high degree of control over their data and security. It is particularly well-suited for teams that require a customizable and scalable file storage and sharing solution, and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and managing their own server.

## Migration Path
1. Export your files from Dropbox using the Dropbox API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up a Nextcloud server, either on-premise or with a hosting provider.
3. Use the Nextcloud import tool to import your files from Dropbox.
4. Configure your Nextcloud server to meet your team's specific needs, including setting up user accounts and permissions.
5. Test your Nextcloud server to ensure that it is working correctly and that all files have been successfully imported.

## Our Take
Nextcloud is a highly capable and customizable file storage and sharing solution, but it may not be production-ready for all users. While it offers a wide range of features and integrations, it can be complex to set up and manage, particularly for users without extensive technical expertise.
One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching to Nextcloud is its limited support for certain file types and formats. While Nextcloud supports a wide range of file types, it may not be compatible with all files, particularly those that are specific to certain industries or applications.
We recommend switching to Nextcloud for teams that require a high degree of control over their data and security, and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and managing their own server. However, for small to medium-sized teams that require a simple and easy-to-use solution, Dropbox may still be the better choice.

## Who Should Switch
* Large teams (50+ users) that require a high degree of control over their data and security
* Teams that do not require a wide range of integrations with third-party apps
* Organizations with strict data ownership and compliance requirements
* Teams with extensive technical expertise and resources
* Users who require a customizable and scalable file storage and sharing solution

## FAQ
### What is the main difference between Dropbox and Nextcloud?
The main difference between Dropbox and Nextcloud is their approach to data ownership and hosting. Dropbox is a proprietary, cloud-based solution, while Nextcloud is an open-source, self-hosted solution.
### Is Nextcloud free?
Yes, Nextcloud is free and open-source. However, users must pay for server costs and maintenance.
### Can I use Nextcloud with my existing Dropbox account?
No, Nextcloud and Dropbox are separate solutions that require separate accounts and setup.
### How do I migrate my files from Dropbox to Nextcloud?
You can migrate your files from Dropbox to Nextcloud using the Nextcloud import tool or a third-party migration service.
### Is Nextcloud compatible with all file types and formats?
No, Nextcloud may not be compatible with all file types and formats, particularly those that are specific to certain industries or applications.
meta_description: Nextcloud, a free self-hosted cloud storage solution, offers greater control and security. See full comparison or Free migration guide.

# Airtable vs NocoDB (2026)

## Overview
Airtable and NocoDB are two popular database management tools used for organizing and tracking data. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and teams who are looking for a reliable and scalable solution for their data management needs, particularly those considering switching from Airtable to a self-hosted alternative like NocoDB. The core use case for both tools is to provide a flexible and customizable database solution, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Airtable offers a free plan and paid plans starting at $10-$20 per user per month, while NocoDB is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: NocoDB allows users to have full ownership and control over their data, while Airtable stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: Airtable has a more user-friendly and intuitive setup process, while NocoDB requires more technical expertise to set up and configure.
* Scalability: NocoDB is highly scalable and can handle large amounts of data, while Airtable's scalability is limited by its pricing plans.
* Feature difference: NocoDB offers a more comprehensive API and customization options, while Airtable has a more user-friendly interface and better integration with other apps.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Airtable | NocoDB |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $10-$20/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $500-$1000/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2000-$4000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Airtable:**
* User-friendly interface and easy setup
* Good integration with other apps and services
* Scalable and reliable
* Limited customization options
* Expensive for large teams
**NocoDB:**
* Highly customizable and scalable
* Self-hosted and free
* Comprehensive API and integration options
* Steeper learning curve and more technical expertise required
* Limited support and community resources

## When to Choose Each
Airtable is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams who need a user-friendly and intuitive database solution with good integration with other apps and services. It is also suitable for teams who are willing to pay a premium for a reliable and scalable solution. On the other hand, NocoDB is a good choice for larger teams or organizations who need a highly customizable and scalable solution with full control over their data. It is also suitable for teams with technical expertise who are looking for a self-hosted solution with low costs.

## Migration Path
1. Export data from Airtable in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up a NocoDB instance on a self-hosted server.
3. Use the NocoDB import tool to import the exported data from Airtable.
4. Configure and customize the NocoDB instance to meet the team's needs.
5. Test and verify the migrated data and functionality.

## Our Take
NocoDB is not yet production-ready for most users due to its limited support and community resources. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that NocoDB requires a high degree of technical expertise to set up and configure. However, for teams who are willing to invest the time and effort, NocoDB offers a highly customizable and scalable solution with full control over their data, and we recommend switching from Airtable to NocoDB for larger teams or organizations with technical expertise.

## Who Should Switch
* Large teams (100+ users) who need a highly customizable and scalable solution
* Organizations with technical expertise who are looking for a self-hosted solution with low costs
* Teams who require full control over their data and are willing to invest time and effort in setup and configuration
* Developers who need a comprehensive API and integration options
* Businesses who are looking for a free and open-source alternative to Airtable
